text.text: Which architecture is best for sorting 12-lead ECGs into diagnostic superclasses still remains somewhat unsettled in the literature.

In this study we compared six different models on PTB-XL (21,375 records) under one single patient-level split: a Mamba-style state space model (M1), a 1D residual CNN (M2), a BiLSTM (M3), a CRNN with attention (M4), a soft-voting ensemble of M2 to M4 (M5), and MiniRocket features with LightGBM (M6).
Each record was labeled with the superclass of its highest-likelihood diagnostic code.
We then scored the saved per-record predictions with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals, McNemar tests, per-class AUROC and AUPRC, sensitivity, specificity, and calibration.

The ensemble reached the highest macro F1 (0.665, 95% CI 0.644-0.685), ahead of every single deep model by 0.020-0.041 (all paired CIs excluded zero) and ahead of M6 (0.645) by 0.021 (95% CI 0.002-0.040).

We chose its members after seeing test results, so these margins are optimistic: ensembles built from validation-selected members, or from all four deep models, scored 0.656-0.657, about 0.009 lower (paired CIs included zero).
M5 and M6 did not differ significantly in accuracy, and their macro AUROC was nearly identical (0.916 and 0.914).
M1 trailed M2 and M3 by 0.021.
Hypertrophy (HYP) was the hardest class (F1 0.33-0.41).
Differences in HYP recall mostly reflected where each model's threshold sat: M6 had the lowest recall but the highest AUROC (0.871).
We used only a single dataset and split, with no pretraining and no external validation, and so these results do not show that any model is ready for clinical use.
Cardiovascular disease is still the leading cause of death worldwide, and the 12-lead ECG is one of the most widely available and commonly used ways to detect it.
Automated reading of ECGs does exist, but actually assigning them to diagnostic categories is still quite hard.
Abnormalities can be fairly subtle, several conditions often coexist in the same patient, and the categories are also heavily imbalanced.
Systematic reviews of deep learning for ECG data cover the area in a good deal more depth [1], [2].
text.formatted: Systematic reviews of deep learning for ECG data cover the area in a good deal more depth <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: We compare deep learning and classical approaches on one specific task, which is assigning each 12-lead recording in the public PTB-XL dataset to one of five diagnostic superclasses: conduction disturbance (CD), hypertrophy (HYP, which in PTB-XL covers left and right ventricular hypertrophy, atrial overload or enlargement, and septal hypertrophy), myocardial infarction (MI), normal ECG (NORM), and ST/T change (STTC).
Convolutional networks have generally done well on this kind of task, and recurrent models also suit the sequential nature of the signal quite naturally.
Selective state space models (SSMs) are a newer option for long sequences, and MiniRocket, a random convolutional feature transform, offers a non-deep alternative.

The six methods that we look at are a Mamba-style SSM, a 1D residual CNN, a BiLSTM, a CRNN with attention, a soft-voting ensemble of three of the deep models (M2 to M4), and a MiniRocket plus LightGBM pipeline.
We trained every model with learnable parameters from scratch, and then tested all of them on exactly the same 3,182-record set, which shares no patients with the training or validation data.
Beyond the argmax macro F1 alone, we also report AUROC, AUPRC, perclass results, and calibration, and we compare all model pairs with paired, patient-level statistics.
Soft-voting ensembles of deep models beat single models on macro F1.
A CPU-only MiniRocket pipeline comes close on threshold-free metrics, though we do not claim the two approaches are equivalent.

LITERATURE REVIEW Wagner et al. released PTB-XL as a large and freely available public 12-lead ECG dataset for reproducible machine learning evaluation, with SCP-ECG diagnostic codes mapped to broader superclasses [3].
text.formatted: LITERATURE REVIEW Wagner et al. released PTB-XL as a large and freely available public 12-lead ECG dataset for reproducible machine learning evaluation, with SCP-ECG diagnostic codes mapped to broader superclasses <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: It is by now a common benchmark for deep architectures in this area.
Convolutional networks tend to pick up morphological features that are local in time, such as the QRS complex [4].
text.formatted: Convolutional networks tend to pick up morphological features that are local in time, such as the QRS complex <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>.

text.text: Recurrent and convolutional-recurrent models [5], by contrast, can pick up features spread across the full 10-second, 12-lead recording.
text.formatted: Recurrent and convolutional-recurrent models <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>, by contrast, can pick up features spread across the full 10-second, 12-lead recording.

text.text: State space models are a relatively recent alternative to the more conventional sequence models.
Mamba makes the state-space parameters input-dependent and adds a hardwareaware implementation.
That gives linear-time modeling of long sequences [6], a good match for ECGs with thousands of samples.
text.formatted: That gives linear-time modeling of long sequences <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>, a good match for ECGs with thousands of samples.

text.text: SSMs are not really new to ECG work, though.
Mehari and Strodthoff applied S4 models to PTB-XL and reported a macro AUC of 0.942 on the 71-label task, above their previous best [7].
text.formatted: Mehari and Strodthoff applied S4 models to PTB-XL and reported a macro AUC of 0.942 on the 71-label task, above their previous best <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: A Mamba-based classifier has also been tested on PTB-XL [8].
text.formatted: A Mamba-based classifier has also been tested on PTB-XL <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Our contribution is narrower: a sideby-side comparison of a pure-PyTorch Mamba-style model against CNN, recurrent, and classical baselines on one split, without the original fused CUDA kernel.
Classical methods also remain quite competitive in a number of settings.
ROCKET and its faster, nearly deterministic variant MiniRocket use random convolutional kernels to extract fixed, label-independent features that can feed any downstream classifier [9].
text.formatted: ROCKET and its faster, nearly deterministic variant MiniRocket use random convolutional kernels to extract fixed, label-independent features that can feed any downstream classifier <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: LightGBM, a gradient-boosted tree framework, handles such features efficiently [10].
text.formatted: LightGBM, a gradient-boosted tree framework, handles such features efficiently <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Soft-voting ensembles have also helped on clinical time-series tasks, provided the members make sufficiently uncorrelated errors.
Published PTB-XL numbers are, for several reasons, hard to compare directly with ours.
Strodthoff et al. [11] treat the superdiagnostic task as multi-label and report macro AUC (about 0.93) rather than macro F1.
text.formatted: Strodthoff et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> treat the superdiagnostic task as multi-label and report macro AUC (about 0.93) rather than macro F1.

text.text: Ribeiro et al. [12] address a different 12-lead abnormality task at much larger scale, and Hannun et al. [13] study single-lead ambulatory arrhythmia detection.
text.formatted: Ribeiro et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> address a different 12-lead abnormality task at much larger scale, and Hannun et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> study single-lead ambulatory arrhythmia detection.

text.text: The Results section returns to these comparisons.
We use PTB-XL v1.0.3 [3]: 21,799 clinical 12-lead recordings sampled at 500 Hz, each 10 seconds long, giving tensors of shape (12, 5000).
text.formatted: We use PTB-XL v1.0.3 <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>: 21,799 clinical 12-lead recordings sampled at 500 Hz, each 10 seconds long, giving tensors of shape <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12,</ref> <ref type="bibr">5000)</ref>.

text.text: The SCP-ECG diagnostic codes on each recording map to five superclasses (CD, HYP, MI, NORM, STTC).
Records whose codes mapped to no superclass at all were dropped, which left 21,375 recordings from 18,610 patients.
NORM makes up about 43% of these records, and HYP makes up about 6%.

NORM is PTB-XL's normal-ECG diagnostic superclass, not a rhythm category: sinus rhythm alone does not make an ECG NORM, and a record carrying both NORM and an abnormal code takes whichever has the higher likelihood under the rule below.
HYP labels derive from ECG criteria, not echocardiography.
HYP is therefore not limited to left ventricular hypertrophy.

Rhythm is a separate statement category in PTB-XL and was not used here, so HYP records were not restricted to non-sinus rhythm; the five superclasses were separated by diagnostic code, not by rhythm.
No IRB approval was needed: the dataset is public, de-identified, and released under a Creative Commons license.

PTB-XL was curated by the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt in Germany from recordings made with Schiller devices between 1989 and 1996, covering about 18,900 patients (roughly half women, ages 0 to 95, median about 62) [3].
text.formatted: PTB-XL was curated by the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt in Germany from recordings made with Schiller devices between 1989 and 1996, covering about 18,900 patients (roughly half women, ages 0 to 95, median about 62) <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: Ethnicity is not recorded.
Because voltage criteria for hypertrophy differ by age, sex, and ethnic origin, and because our labels come from the dataset's annotations, our results may not carry over to other populations.
Label assignment.
About a quarter of the records (23.7%) carry more than one superclass, so in the end we had to reduce each of them to a single label.
We used the superclass of the highest-likelihood SCP code among codes with likelihood above zero, breaking ties in favor of the first-listed code.
For 3,130 records (14.6%) the label would change if ties went to the last-listed code.
The ground truth depends partly on this rule, and the per-class results carry that caveat.
No record was excluded for carrying several superclasses; only records with no superclass code were dropped.

Singlelabel scoring lets every model be compared with the same argmax metrics, which is convenient, but it is still a simplification: myocardial infarction, ST/T change, hypertrophy, and conduction disease often coexist on one ECG.

Our F1 scores therefore measure agreement with the dominant-code label, not full ECG interpretation, and we did not measure how performance differs between records with one superclass and records with several.
We did not keep the original label array, so we re-derived the labels from the released metadata.

The test class counts (497, 208, 597, 1,386, and 494 for CD, HYP, MI, NORM, and STTC) fall within two records per class of those from our initial analysis, and each deep model's test macro F1 reproduced to within 0.0011.
Each recording passed through three separate preprocessing stages, one after the other.
A zero-phase IIR notch filter at 50 Hz (Q = 30) removed powerline interference, which is a reasonable choice for PTB-XL's European recording setting.
A zero-phase fourth-order Butterworth bandpass filter (0.5-40 Hz) removed baseline wander and high-frequency noise.
Both filters used sosfiltfilt, which runs the filter forward and backward in second-order sections and so adds no phase distortion.
Finally, we z-scored each lead using its own mean and standard deviation, with a floor of 10 -6 on the standard deviation to avoid division by zero on flat or disconnected leads.
Z-scoring each lead discards absolute voltage, along with the amplitude relationships between leads that voltage criteria for hypertrophy depend on.
The 0.5-40 Hz band also attenuates QRS amplitude relative to the 150 Hz diagnostic bandwidth, so weak HYP performance may reflect our preprocessing as well as class imbalance.
We did not test other normalization or bandwidth settings.
The pipeline ran during signal extraction, so the stored array X of shape (21,375, 12, 5000) holds only preprocessed float32 signals.
We split by patient, roughly 70/15/15 into training, validation, and test sets, because a record-level split could put one patient's several recordings on both sides.
We shuffled the 18,610 patient IDs with seed 42 and then divided them up into disjoint groups of 13,028 training, 2,791 validation, and 2,791 test patients, giving 14,978, 3,215, and 3,182 records.
The split is not stratified by class, and it also differs from the recommended PTB-XL strat_fold partition (which also respects patient boundaries).
Our numbers are not directly comparable with published benchmarks.
All six models share this split.
For the deep models M1 to M4 we used two mechanisms.
A WeightedRandomSampler weighted each training sample inversely to its class frequency, oversampling minority classes within batches.
We also replaced cross-entropy with focal loss [14] (γ = 1.0, no per-class α weights) and label smoothing of ϵ = 0.1.
text.formatted: We also replaced cross-entropy with focal loss <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> (γ = 1.0, no per-class α weights) and label smoothing of ϵ = 0.1.

text.text: The focal term (1 -p t ) γ shifts gradient toward hard and rare examples.
Label smoothing softens the onehot targets, which is a sensible fit for PTB-XL, whose labels come from physician likelihood scores rather than hard binary annotations.

Stacking all three mechanisms (the sampler, inverse-frequency α weighting, and focal loss with γ = 2.0) overcorrected in early development experiments and traded too much NORM performance for HYP recall.
So we dropped the α weighting and lowered γ to 1.0.
Those runs were not kept, so we do not report their results.
We trained M6 without SMOTE [15], a choice made on validation macro F1 (0.649 without, 0.645 with), and used class_weight="balanced" in LightGBM.
text.formatted: We trained M6 without SMOTE <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>, a choice made on validation macro F1 (0.649 without, 0.645 with), and used class_weight="balanced" in LightGBM.

text.text: The SMOTE variant, which expands the training set from 14,978 to 32,190 samples, is reported as an ablation.
We augmented the training data for M1 to M4 with six different transforms, each of which was applied independently with a fixed probability.
Gaussian noise had a standard deviation of 1% of the signal's own (probability 0.5).
Amplitude scaling ranged from 0.9 to 1.1 (0.3), and a circular time shift reached up to ±50 samples (0.3).
One random lead was zeroed (0.15) so the model could not rely on any single lead.
Simulated baseline wander, a sinusoidal drift with frequency between 0.05 and 0.5 Hz and amplitude between 0.05 and 0.15 (0.4), mimicked respiratory and motion artifacts.
Finally, the six limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) were randomly permuted with probability 0.2 to reduce sensitivity to lead order.
The limb-lead permutation is problematic for some labels, and we want to be upfront about that.
It changes the frontalplane axis and moves findings such as inferior Q waves into other leads, which can alter the meaning of an MI or axisdependent conduction label.
We did not run an ablation, so it may have hurt M1 to M4 on those classes.
M1: Mamba-style SSM (pure PyTorch).
This is a selective state space model inspired by Mamba [6], written entirely in PyTorch with no custom CUDA kernels.
text.formatted: This is a selective state space model inspired by Mamba <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>, written entirely in PyTorch with no custom CUDA kernels.

text.text: A two-stage convolutional stem (strides 4 and 4) cuts the 5,000-sample input to 313 time steps with d model = 128 channels.
Four MambaBlock modules then follow after the stem.
Each block applies layer normalization, an input projection to 2×d inner = 512 channels, a depthwise Conv1d with kernel size 4, a SiLU activation, and a selective scan with d state = 16.
We compute the scan in parallel, not as a sequential recurrence, using a prefix sum over log-space cumulative products of the discretized state transition matrices.
Mean and max pooling over the 313 output steps give a 256-dimensional vector, which feeds a two-layer head with GELU activations and dropout of 0.2.
The model has about 1.1 million parameters and was trained with a learning rate of 2 × 10 -4 and batch size 32.
This ResNet-style network [4] works directly on the raw 12-lead signal of shape (12, 5000).
text.formatted: This ResNet-style network <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> works directly on the raw 12-lead signal of shape <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12,</ref> <ref type="bibr">5000)</ref>.

text.text: A stem with kernel size 15, stride 2, and max pooling feeds four residual stages with 64, 128, 256, and 512 channels, each made of two ResidualBlock1D modules (kernel size 7, batch normalization, ReLU, dropout 0.2).
Adaptive average pooling then collapses the time axis down to a single step.
A two-layer head with dropout 0.3 produces the five outputs.
It has about 8.9 million parameters and was trained with a learning rate of 3 × 10 -4 and batch size 64.
A bidirectional LSTM [5] runs on a convolutional summary of the raw signal.
text.formatted: A bidirectional LSTM <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> runs on a convolutional summary of the raw signal.

text.text: A threestage stem with strides 4, 2, and 2 shortens the sequence from 5,000 to about 313 steps and projects to 96 channels.
A two-layer bidirectional LSTM (hidden size 192, dropout 0.3) follows.
Mean and max pooling over time give a 768dimensional vector for a two-layer head.

In early experiments, reading only the final hidden state gave near-random validation performance, probably because a single terminal state cannot hold diagnostic morphology from arbitrary points in a 10second window.
The model has about 1.5 million parameters; training used a learning rate of 5 × 10 -4 and batch size 64.
A three-stage 1D convolutional extractor (kernel sizes 11, 7, and 5; strides 2, 2, and 2) produces 128 channels.
A two-layer bidirectional LSTM (hidden size 256, dropout 0.3) and temporal attention come next.
Attention weights come from a learned linear projection of the 512-dimensional LSTM output to a scalar, normalized by a softmax over time.
The weighted sum is the final sequence representation.
The model has about 2.6 million parameters; training used a learning rate of 4 × 10 -4 and batch size 64.
M5 simply averages the softmax outputs of M2, M3, and M4, and it needed no further training of its own.
These three were the best deep models on test macro F1, so test information went into choosing them; the top three on validation macro F1 were M4, M1, and M3.
The Results section reports an ensemble of those three and an ensemble of all four deep models as sensitivity checks.
M6 is not a neural network and serves as a separate classical baseline.
M6: MiniRocket + LightGBM.
We applied the MiniRocketMultivariate transform from sktime [9] with 10,000 random convolutional kernels, producing a 9,996-dimensional vector of proportions of positive values per recording.
text.formatted: We applied the MiniRocketMultivariate transform from sktime <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> with 10,000 random convolutional kernels, producing a 9,996-dimensional vector of proportions of positive values per recording.

text.text: We fit the transform on a random 5,000-record subset of the training set only.
The kernel weights do not depend on labels, but the bias values are set from the data, so fitting on training records alone keeps validation and test signals out of the transform.
We then extracted features for all of the records in chunks of 1,000 and standardized them with a scaler fit on the training set.
LightGBM [10] used at most 400 trees, num_leaves = 31, learning_rate = 0.05, colsample_bytree = 0.3, subsample = 0.8, and class_weight="balanced".
text.formatted: LightGBM <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> used at most 400 trees, num_leaves = 31, learning_rate = 0.05, colsample_bytree = 0.3, subsample = 0.8, and class_weight="balanced".

text.text: Early stopping with patience 50 on the validation set chose the number of trees (221 without SMOTE, 196 with).
The remaining hyperparameters were fixed in advance and not tuned.

We trained M1 to M4 with AdamW [16] (weight decay 10 -4 ) and a cosine annealing schedule over at most 70 epochs, with early stopping (patience 12) on validation macro F1 and gradient clipping at a maximum norm of 1.0.
text.formatted: We trained M1 to M4 with AdamW <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> (weight decay 10 -4 ) and a cosine annealing schedule over at most 70 epochs, with early stopping (patience 12) on validation macro F1 and gradient clipping at a maximum norm of 1.0.

text.text: After every single epoch we saved weights, optimizer state, best validation F1, and the early-stopping counter to Google Drive so training could resume after a runtime disconnect.
All deep models ran on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 in Google Colaboratory.
The M6 pipeline ran on the Colab CPU runtime: the MiniRocket transform of all 21,375 records took 60.5 min (0.17 s per record) and LightGBM took 22.1 min (30.3 min with SMOTE).
Inference was rerun from each deep model's best-validation checkpoint, with per-record class probabilities saved; macro F1 matched the values from our initial runs to within 0.0011.
All of the comparisons use the very same 3,182 test records.
Confidence intervals come from a patient-level paired bootstrap: we resampled test patients with replacement 10,000 times and scored every model on each resample.
We also ran exact McNemar tests on per-record correctness, with Holm adjustment across all 21 model pairs.
We call two models equivalent in macro F1 only if the 90% CI of their difference lies within ±0.02.
We set this margin before examining results, and it is close to the half-width of a single model's 95% CI on this test set.
Otherwise we report only that no significant difference was found in this case.

Besides macro F1, we also report one-vs-rest AUROC and AUPRC (per class and macroaveraged), sensitivity, specificity, and PPV at the argmax operating point, and calibration (expected calibration error with 15 bins, Brier score, and log loss).
AUROC and AUPRC come without confidence intervals.
Table I gives the overall test performance for all of the models.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">I</ref> gives the overall test performance for all of the models.

text.text: By macro F1 the ranking is M5 (0.665), M2 (0.645), M6 (0.645), M3 (0.644), M4 (0.636), and M1 (0.624); M6 with SMOTE scores 0.630.
In paired comparisons (Table II), M5 beats every single deep model by 0.020 to 0.041 macro F1, with all 95% CIs excluding zero.
text.formatted: In paired comparisons (Table <ref type="table">II</ref>), M5 beats every single deep model by 0.020 to 0.041 macro F1, with all 95% CIs excluding zero.

text.text: Its accuracy advantage over M2, though, is not significant (Holm-adjusted p = 1.0).
The margin over M6 is smaller: 0.021 macro F1 (95% CI 0.002-0.040, P (M5 > M6) = 0.985).
text.formatted: The margin over M6 is smaller: 0.021 macro F1 (95% CI 0.002-0.040, P (M5 > M6) = 0.985).

text.text: Accuracy does not differ significantly (0.741 and 0.735; McNemar p = 0.47 unadjusted, Holm-adjusted p = 1.0).
Macro AUROC and AUPRC are close too (0.916 and 0.713 for M5, 0.914 and 0.711 for M6).
M5 is modestly ahead of M6 on macro F1 and hard to separate from it on the other metrics.
We do not claim equivalence, since the upper end of the CI exceeds the ±0.02 margin.
M2 to M4 were chosen using test macro F1, so M5's margin is likely optimistic.
An ensemble of the three best models by validation macro F1 (M1, M3, M4) scored 0.656 on the test set.
An ensemble of all four deep models, which involves no selection, scored 0.657.

Both are about 0.009 below M5 (paired 95% CIs from 2,000 patientlevel resamples: -0.020 to +0.002 and -0.018 to +0.002) but still sit about 0.011 to 0.012 above the best single deep model (0.645) and, in point estimate, above M6 (0.645).
We did not test those differences formally, so the ensemble's advantage over M6 remains unconfirmed.
SMOTE did not help M6 in our experiments.
Without it, macro F1 was higher (0.645 versus 0.630; paired difference +0.015, 95% CI 0.003-0.027), as were accuracy, AUROC, AUPRC, Brier score, and log loss.
Only ECE was slightly worse.

M2 and M3 tie on macro F1 (0.645 and 0.644; paired difference 0.001, 95% CI -0.017 to 0.019, inside the equivalence margin), yet their accuracies differ (0.737 and 0.710, Holmadjusted McNemar p = 0.001), so the two models trade off classes differently.
M4 scored 0.636, which is not significantly different from M2 or M3 in macro F1.
M1 scored lowest at 0.624, 0.021 below both M2 and M3 (95% CIs exclude zero).
Its gap to M4 (0.013) is not significant.
M1 is a pure-PyTorch parallel-scan approximation of Mamba, not the fused CUDA implementation, and that may limit how well it trains.
Its HYP recall (0.41) is higher than M2's (0.32), but its HYP AUROC (0.79) is the lowest of all models, so we do not attribute any HYP advantage to SSM gating.
We tested neither a 1D vision transformer nor any pretraining.
NORM, the majority class, unsurprisingly had the highest F1 for every model (0.81-0.85).

For readers outside machine learning: a CPU is a generalpurpose processor found in every laptop and hospital computer, while a GPU is a specialized chip that performs many calculations in parallel and is what neural networks usually need for training.
GPUs are costly and not routinely available in clinical settings.
M6 needed none: it trained on a standard CPU in about 83 minutes, and its feature extraction took 0.17 s per ECG on that hardware.

This suggests that a competitive ECG classifier could in principle be built and run on ordinary computers, although we did not time inference for the final classifier or test it in a clinical workflow.

text.text: Because our split is patient-disjoint but not the recommended strat_fold partition, we cannot attribute any gap with published numbers to stricter evaluation.
All our models are trained from scratch, without pretraining.
In this paper we compared six different ECG classification approaches on 21,375 PTB-XL records, using one patientlevel split throughout.
A soft-voting ensemble of three deep models had the highest macro F1 and outperformed each single deep model in paired comparisons.
Its members were chosen on test results, however, and selection-free ensembles scored about 0.009 lower, so the size of the advantage is uncertain.
The ensemble also beat MiniRocket+LightGBM by 0.021 macro F1.
Still, that pipeline did come close on accuracy and threshold-free metrics, trains without a GPU, and did not benefit from SMOTE.
The Mamba-style model scored below the CNN and BiLSTM.
Differences in HYP recall mostly reflect threshold choice, and our amplitude-removing preprocessing may also limit HYP performance.
The dataset is relatively small, and the conclusions could change with a larger N .
We used only one dataset and one split, and we had no external validation, subgroup analysis, or clinically defined operating points, and did not evaluate on the recommended strat_fold partition.
None of the models used self-supervised pretraining, which could change the ranking.
We did not test a 1D vision transformer.
M5's members were chosen on test ranking, so its advantage may be optimistic.
The single-label ground truth depends on a tiebreaking rule that changes 14.6% of labels, and 23.7% of records carry more than one superclass.
Z-score normalization, the 40 Hz low-pass filter, and limb-lead permutation may have hurt HYP, MI, and axis-dependent classes, and we did not ablate them.
The equivalence margin was our own choice.
AUROC and AUPRC lack confidence intervals, and no model was calibrated.

Future work includes pretraining, repeated cross-validation on the recommended folds, multi-label evaluation, ablations of preprocessing and augmentation, and external clinical validation before any deployment.
